'''Didier Stainier''' (born 1963) is a Belgian/American developmental [[geneticist]] who is currently a director at the Max Planck Institute for Heart and Lung Research in Bad Nauheim, Germany.<ref>{{cite web|title=Board of Directors, MPI for Heart and Lung Research|url=https://www.mpi-hlr.de/institute/board-of-directors|url-status=live|website=mpi-hlr.de|accessdate=17 June 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201130075638/https://www.mpi-hlr.de/institute/board-of-directors |archive-date=2020-11-30 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Bio on the Max Planck Society's website|url=https://www.mpg.de/6661546/herz_lungenforschung_wissM11|website=mpg.de|accessdate=4 February 2018}}</ref>

==Scientific career==
Didier Stainier studied [[biology]] in Wales [[Atlantic College|(United World College of the Atlantic)]], Belgium ([[University of Liège]]) and the USA ([[Brandeis University]]) where he got a BA in 1984. He has a PhD in [[biochemistry]] and [[biophysics]] from [[Harvard University]] (1990).  During his PhD work, he investigated [[axon guidance]] and target recognition in the developing mouse with [[Walter Gilbert]].  Subsequently, he initiated the studies on [[zebrafish]] [[heart development|cardiac development]] as a Helen Hay Whitney postdoctoral fellow with [[Mark Fishman]] at the [[Massachusetts General Hospital]] (Boston).

===Scientific interests===
Together with the many students and postdocs in his laboratory, Stainier helped pioneer the use of the [[zebrafish]] [[model organism|model]] to study a wide range of questions pertaining to [[vertebrate]] organ development and function,<ref>{{cite web|title=Transparent eggs of the zebra fish let researchers see how DNA directs embryonic development|url=http://www.sfgate.com/science/article/Window-On-Life-Transparent-eggs-of-the-zebra-3240679.php#photo-2387603|website=sfgate.com|date=7 February 2000 |accessdate=4 February 2018}}</ref> and has published extensively.<ref>{{cite web |title=Search results for author Stainier D |url=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=stainier+d |website=on [[PubMed]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Scopus - author information|url=https://www.scopus.com/authid/detail.uri?authorId=7005076881|website=scopus.com|accessdate=4 February 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Google Scholars - author information|url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=2rEmOPwAAAAJ|website=scholar.google.com|accessdate=4 February 2018}}</ref> His [[forward genetics|forward genetic]] analyses of heart development revealed the unexpected role of several [[signaling pathways]] including [[sphingosine 1-phosphate]] signaling<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1038/35018092 |pmid=10910360 |title=A sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor regulates cell migration during vertebrate heart development |journal=Nature |volume=406 |issue=6792 |pages=192–5 |year=2000 |last1=Kupperman |first1=Erik |last2=An |first2=Songzhu |last3=Osborne |first3=Nick |last4=Waldron |first4=Steven |last5=Stainier |first5=Didier Y. R |bibcode=2000Natur.406..192K |s2cid=4412483 }}</ref> and the discovery of the long-elusive sphingosine 1-phosphate transporter.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.cub.2008.10.061 |pmid=19062281 |pmc=2741689 |title=The Spinster Homolog, Two of Hearts, is Required for Sphingosine 1-Phosphate Signaling in Zebrafish |journal=Current Biology |volume=18 |issue=23 |pages=1882–8 |year=2008
